sections.title: Where Income Misleads
sections.intro: Median income is an area average. Four things to check before it drives a targeting change.

items.title: High Income Is Not Homeownership
items.text: Income and owner occupancy correlate at only {incomeOwnerCorr} across ZIP codes with 500 or more households. {renterTargets} target ZIPs holding {renterTargetHouseholds:int} households are majority renter. For home and bundle campaigns, check the Homeownership layer.

items.title: Students and Transient Workers
items.text: College ZIP codes post very low medians that describe students, not the local market. Energy and military ZIP codes can pass an income screen on a workforce that does not stay. Judge both on the agency's own results, not their income rank.

items.title: The Estimate Is Soft
items.text: ACS 5-year values pool 60 months of responses from 2020 to 2024. The median ZIP margin of error is {medianMoe}% of the estimate, and {highMoeZips} ZIP codes are at {coreMaxMoe}% or more. That is why the core list drops small and noisy ZIPs.

items.title: Income Stands In for Lead Facts
items.text: Prior coverage, credit-based insurance score, driving record and homeowner status decide whether a lead quotes and binds. Where a source filters on currently insured or homeowner, that filter acts on the cause. A ZIP income screen acts on a correlate.

sections.title: Putting It to Work
sections.intro: The best use of this list is as a measuring tool for an agency's own leads.

items.title: Measure by Quartile First
items.text: Tag each lead with its ZIP's income quartile and core status, then compare contact, quote and bind rates by quartile, by line and by source. A step-down across sources supports a geographic test. Flat rates point to price or sales process.

items.title: Trim the Bottom Before the Middle
items.text: If the results support a change, deprioritize the weakest bottom-quartile ZIPs before restricting to the top. The third quartile holds {thirdShare}% of Texas households, too much volume to cut on no evidence.

items.title: Run Core ZIPs as Their Own Segment
items.text: Give the {coreZips} core ZIPs their own segment and bid so their results read apart from the rest of the campaign. Leave out the {lowConfZips} low-confidence ZIPs and keep to the agency's service area.

items.title: Keep the Rule Explainable
items.text: Insurance law limits refusing or pricing coverage by geography, ad platforms can restrict ZIP targeting for insurance, and an income screen can track race and ethnicity. A rule grounded in the agency's own results and homeownership is easier to explain than income alone. This is not legal advice.

methods.title: Median Household Income
methods.text: ACS 2020-2024 5-year table B19013 for every ZIP Code Tabulation Area and county, in 2024 dollars, with its margin of error. {zipsSuppressed} ZIP codes with too few responses have no published median; they hold {suppressedShare}% of households.

methods.title: Quartiles and the Target List
methods.text: ZIP codes with a published median, each counted once, are cut at the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles: {q1:money}, {q2:money} and {q3:money}. The top quartile is the target list. Counties get their own quartiles across the {counties} Texas counties.

methods.title: Core Target ZIPs
methods.text: A target ZIP with at least {coreMinHouseholds} households and a margin of error under {coreMaxMoe}% of the estimate. Top-coded medians ($250,000 or more) have no margin and pass on households alone. The other {lowConfZips} target ZIPs are flagged low confidence.

methods.title: Counties, Metros and ZIPs
methods.text: Each ZIP code takes the county holding the largest share of its land (Census 2020 relationship file) and that county's metro area (OMB July 2023 delineation). ZIP areas are Census ZCTAs, so PO-box-only ZIPs and ZIPs created after 2020 have no row. Town names from GeoNames.
